title: A Data-free Universal Prior over Syntactic Structures
abstract: Probability is fundamental to theories of language comprehension, production, acquisition, and evolution, as well as to large language models. Existing theories estimate the probability of syntactic structures from language-specific data. Whether part of this probability structure can arise independently of language-specific experience remains unknown. Here I show that a universal prior over syntactic structures emerges from a cognitively motivated model of incremental language production, in which words are progressively integrated into syntactic structure through network growth. The resulting prior assigns probabilities to syntactic structures --represented as dependency trees-- without fitting parameters to linguistic data, and assigns higher probabilities to attested than to random trees in all 138 typologically diverse languages examined. These prior probabilities correlate positively with probabilities estimated from corpora in 33 of 34 languages. The results indicate that part of the probability structure of syntax can arise independently of language-specific statistical learning. Linguistic experience may therefore refine probabilities that are already structured by the process of language production, rather than create them from an initially uniform space. This identifies a possible cognitive origin for part of the probability distribution over syntactic structures, linking language production and statistical learning while providing a data-independent structural bias for probabilistic models of language.
summary: This work proposes that a universal, data-free prior exists for syntactic structures, derived from modeling the cognitive process of language production. By comparing this theoretical prior against probabilities derived from dozens of real languages, the authors show a strong correlation, suggesting that language structure is partially constrained by universal generative principles rather than solely by accumulated linguistic experience.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the probability structure of syntactic rules can arise independently of language-specific statistical learning, suggesting a universal, data-free prior.
main_result: A universal prior derived from a cognitively motivated model of language production shows a strong positive correlation with probabilities estimated from actual linguistic data across many typologically diverse languages.
method: The authors compare the probabilities derived from a data-free sublinear preferential attachment (sPA) prior against probabilities estimated using Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) for various languages.
model_or_system: The model is a cognitively motivated process of incremental language production, where syntactic structures are built up as a growing network (dependency tree). The probability is calculated by integrating over attachment parameters and production orderings.
key_observables: Correlation coefficients between the universal sPA prior probability and language-specific PCFG probabilities; the linear regression coefficient (beta) linking these two measures.
important_parameters: The sublinear attachment exponent $\alpha$ (integrated over a Beta(2, 2) prior); the number of nodes $n$ in the dependency tree.
main_assumptions: The underlying generative process follows an approximately incremental sublinear preferential attachment model, and language-specific probabilities are adequately approximated by PCFGs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the probability advantage of the sPA model over a uniform prior, and show the positive correlation between the sPA prior and language-specific PCFG probabilities across many languages.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of data-independent syntactic priors, develops the sPA model based on incremental production, calculates the universal prior via Monte Carlo integration, and finally tests this prior by correlating its predictions against empirical PCFG estimates across a large, diverse dataset of languages.
why_interesting: While focused on linguistics, the methodology involves complex statistical inference, modeling emergent structure from local rules (preferential attachment), and comparing theoretical priors against empirical data, which shares conceptual overlap with modeling complex systems in condensed matter or neural networks.
